title: The beginning (Mark 1:1–8)
hook: no birth story, just the beginning of the good news and a voice in the desert

segments.voice: Yesterday, Alleluia, and the Psalms ended with everything that breathes. That was your line. Today, a new book, read straight through.

Most stories about a famous person start with a birth: a baby, a family, a hometown, a childhood. Matthew and Luke do that: angels, shepherds, wise men, a stable. Mark doesn't. No manger. No star. No Mary and Joseph on the road. Mark opens with one line, like a title card at the start of a film, then drops you straight into the desert, where a wild man in camel's hair is shouting at crowds. For forty days, it's Mark start to finish, a few verses at a time. Today's word is in his first sentence: gospel.
screen: `NO MANGER. NO STAR.` → `ONE LINE, LIKE A TITLE CARD.` → `FORTY DAYS OF MARK.`

segments.voice: First, the line. In the Douay-Rheims: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God." That's the whole first verse. Mark says what he's writing and who it's about, and wastes no words. Second, the word. Gospel comes from old English, god-spel, good story, good news. Mark wrote in Greek, and his word is euangelion. In his world it was the word for big public news: a victory announced, a new emperor, a royal birth, sent out by messengers to every town. Greek Isaiah used the same root for heralds running ahead of God, and Paul was already using the word for the message about Jesus. Mark sets it over the whole story: this is the real headline. Third, the voice. Mark quotes the prophets: "A voice of one crying in the desert: Prepare ye the way of the Lord, make straight his paths." And there's John the Baptist, living rough in camel's hair with a leather belt, eating locusts and wild honey, calling people to be baptized in the Jordan and turn their lives around. Crowds come from the whole countryside and from Jerusalem. Then John points away from himself: someone mightier is coming after me; I'm not worthy to stoop down and untie his sandals. Fourth, the book. Mark is the shortest of the four gospels. Many scholars think it was the first written, and an early tradition says Mark set down what he'd heard Peter preach. You can read it aloud in about two hours. It moves fast, as tomorrow shows.
screen: `THE BEGINNING OF THE GOSPEL.` · `EUANGELION: PUBLIC GOOD NEWS.` · `A VOICE CRYING IN THE DESERT.` · `THE SHORTEST GOSPEL, AND FAST.` · then, large: `PREPARE YE THE WAY OF THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Find Mark chapter one, verse one, in a Bible or on your phone, or use the words you heard: the beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God. Say it out loud, slowly, the way a herald would announce news in a town square. Then sit with it: what would good news sound like, for you, today? If you pray, you can offer that.
Gospel. Old English for good news, from the Greek euangelion, the word for news big enough to send heralds. Today's word.
Your line: gospel means good news. One headline, and the story is off and running. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: At Mass, Catholics stand for the Gospel, trace a small cross on forehead, lips and heart as it is announced, and hear it read by a deacon or priest; the Gospel of Mark is read on most Sundays in Year B of the lectionary.

chat.says: Why does Mark call his book a gospel? Isn't that just a church word?
options: It means good news, the word for big headlines heralds carried to every town.
It means holy rule book, the laws Christians are meant to follow.
It means a birth story, since every gospel starts with the baby Jesus.
chat.meaning: Gospel is Old English for good news. Mark's Greek word, euangelion, was the word for public news big enough to send heralds.

Part open: first day of Part 2 (The Gospel of Mark, straight through, days 192–231, forty days).
Etymology: gospel from Old English godspel (good + spel, news/story); confirm.

Euangelion in imperial usage (e.g. the Priene calendar inscription for Augustus): common scholarly point; stated generally. 'Mark may be the first to use it as the title of a book' in the trapdoor is a scholarly suggestion; confirm phrasing.
Markan priority stated as 'many scholars think'; the Papias tradition that Mark wrote down Peter's preaching is cited.
'Read aloud in about two hours': estimates vary (roughly 1.5–2 hours); confirm.
howItsDone: Mark is the main Sunday gospel in Year B; confirm.

Audit (second sample): the teach said euangelion 'wasn't a religious word yet' in Mark's world. That is wrong: Paul's letters, written before Mark, already use it for the Christian message, Greek Isaiah uses the verb (euangelizomai) for heralds of God's coming (e.g. Isaiah 40:9; 52:7), and the imperial usage itself was religious (Augustus as divine). The teach and trapdoor now say so; the public-news sense is kept.
